recentItems.title: Iran-Gulf talks in Oman could reshape regional alliances, analyst says
recentItems.description:
Gulf states are preparing to meet with Iran in Oman on Monday, as the war between the US and Iran continues to reshape regional alliances and force countries in the region to rethink their reliance on Washington. Iran is expected to outline its expectations at the meeting, with most Gulf states planning to attend, though Bahrain is not. Against that backdrop, Mohamed Elmasry, professor at the Doha Institute for Graduate Studies, told Al Jazeera that it remains unclear whether the Oman meeting will resemble an “Iranian lecture” or a genuine give-and-take dialogue where Gulf states can express their concerns and find middle ground. He said the more important question is what happens if the Gulf states and Iran do reach an understanding, and how Donald Trump and the United States would react. Elmasry cited a Wall Street Journal report that Trump’s top advisers, including Marco Rubio and JD Vance, have told him the war could last through the midterms and possibly the rest of his term, suggesting Gulf states may realise they have to take matters into their own hands. On Trump’s claim that the Houthis called him asking America not to intervene in Yemen, Elmasry said it signals the US will not get involved and that Trump has no interest in opening a new front. He said there appears to be an implicit understanding that if others stay out, the Bab al-Mandeb Strait will remain open to everyone except the Saudis, which could be catastrophic for the global economy. Elmasry added that Gulf countries are frustrated and rethinking their relationship with the US after warning Trump of the consequences before the war, and are now engaging directly with Iran, which he described as “stunning”.

recentItems.title: Two injured in Saudi city of Jizan as Saudi government accuses Yemen's Houthis of attack
recentItems.description:
Two people were injured after an incoming projectile struck a residential area in the Saudi city of Jizan, with a mosque, vehicles and buildings damaged. Saudi Arabia accused the Ansar Allah Houthis of carrying out the attack, but the group has not claimed responsibility. The incident comes as Saudi Arabia and Yemen's internationally recognised government forces intensify attacks against the Houthis, with more strikes reported in recent hours. The fighting spans a broad stretch of Yemen's Red Sea coast but is centred on the battle for control of the critical Bab al-Mandeb Strait, a vital maritime choke point for global shipping. Government forces said they carried out more than 20 raids on Houthi sites, rocket launch platforms and vehicles, seeking to retake the strategic port of Mocha, which was seized by Houthi fighters on Thursday. The Houthis accused Saudi Arabia of launching more than 100 air strikes on Yemen within the past 48 hours and claimed they launched a missile and drone attack on a Saudi military base in the Sharurah region, warning that continued Saudi attacks would provoke larger strikes deeper inside Saudi territory. 

Al Jazeera's Yousef Mawry reports from Sanaa.

recentItems.title: Kyrgyzstan's melting glaciers threaten water supplies across Central Asia
recentItems.description:
Kyrgyzstan's 10,000 glaciers, known as central Asia's "water tower," are retreating rapidly, with some losing up to 16 metres annually. The country has recorded nearly 1,000 flood and mudflow emergencies since 2015, while 368 glacial lakes are now considered at risk of dangerous outburst floods. Scientists warn that mining, infrastructure expansion and global warming are accelerating the crisis, threatening water supplies for farming, hydropower and downstream nations including Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan.

Al Jazeera’s Osama bin Javaid reports from Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan.

recentItems.title: Bangsamoro holds first election as fears of renewed conflict linger
recentItems.description:
The Muslim-majority Bangsamoro region in the southern Philippines is holding its first parliamentary election, the final step in its transition to self-governance. The separatist Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF) signed a peace deal with the government in 2014, ending decades of conflict, and has run the region under an interim government since 2019. Now it is contesting 80 seats in the new parliament.

Peace has remained fragile: in 2016, ISIL-linked fighters briefly seized one town, and in August, Bangsamoro's chief minister survived an ambush, prompting checkpoints across the region. Poverty has halved under MILF's interim rule, but Bangsamoro remains one of the Philippines' poorest regions. Political dynasties that governed before 2019 are also contesting seats, arguing they can better serve their communities. Voters say lasting peace remains the only path to progress.

Al Jazeera's Barnaby Lo reports from Butig, Lanao del Sur, in the southern Philippines.

recentItems.title: Inside Sinaloa's cartel war, two years on and no end in sight | Inside Latin America
recentItems.description:
Two years ago this week, the betrayal and kidnapping of Sinaloa Cartel boss Ismael "El Mayo" Zambada by rival Joaquin Guzman, who flew him to the US as a bargaining chip, ignited a civil war within the cartel that has convulsed the state ever since.

Since then, thousands have been killed or disappeared, with searchers like the volunteer group Sabuesos Guerreras digging through the countryside using little more than metal ground drills, often without government support. Criminals here have a saying: "If there's no body, there's no crime."

Al Jazeera's John Holman reports from Culiacan.

recentItems.title: Trump says he'd 'love' a united Ireland as visit draws protests
recentItems.description:
US President Donald Trump has met Ireland's leaders during a visit in which he said he would "love" to see a united Ireland and discussed the war with Iran. The visit drew protests in Dublin and in the west, where Trump travelled to his golf resort for the Irish Open.

Polls suggest Trump is deeply unpopular in Ireland, and protesters marched through central Dublin to parliament, objecting to his visit and, in some cases, to Irish leaders meeting him given Ireland's stance on Palestine. By afternoon, Trump was in Doonbeg, where his resort brings welcome business, and he is popular. Despite divided opinion, few in Ireland dispute the importance of the US relationship.

Al Jazeera's Milena Veselinovic reports from Dublin.
